analysis.one_liner: Expands federal workplace safety law to government workers, raises employer penalties, and makes employers pay for protective gear.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and its subcommittee in 2007 and never received a House vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 to cover federal, state, and local government employees, who are largely outside the law today [S2][S3]. It strengthens whistleblower protections so workers who report injuries or unsafe conditions can get reinstatement, back pay, and compensatory damages [S3]. It raises civil fines — willful violations from a $70,000 maximum to $100,000, up to $250,000 when a worker dies, and routine serious violations from $7,000 to $10,000 — and raises criminal penalties for willful violations that kill a worker from a maximum of six months in prison to ten years, and up to twenty years for repeat offenders [S3]. It also requires employers to provide personal protective equipment at no cost to workers and gives injured workers and bereaved families rights in OSHA investigations and settlements [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million state and local government employees not covered by federal OSHA, plus private-sector workers who gain stronger protection against retaliation, free protective equipment, and investigations and penalties with enough teeth to change employer behavior. Families of workers killed on the job gain a formal role in investigations and settlement decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Government employees and workers in unsafe jobs

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA coverage to federal, state, and local government employees, a group the 1970 law excludes [S2][S3].
Lets workers file retaliation complaints within 180 days and win reinstatement, back pay, compensatory damages, and attorney's fees through a streamlined Labor Department process [S3].

Raises civil penalties: willful or repeated violations from $70,000 to $100,000 maximum, $250,000 when a violation kills a worker, and standard serious violations from $7,000 to $10,000, with amounts adjusted for inflation every four years [S3].

Raises criminal penalties for willful safety violations: up to 10 years for a first offense causing death, up to 20 years for repeat offenses, and creates a new crime — up to 5 years — for willful violations causing serious bodily injury [S3].
Requires employers to provide and pay for personal protective equipment such as respirators, gloves, and harnesses, ending the practice of charging workers for gear [S2][S3].

Mandates investigations of every workplace death and of incidents hospitalizing two or more workers, and gives injured workers and surviving families rights to meet with investigators, receive citations, and object before citations are withdrawn in settlements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, in three ways: higher fines and real criminal exposure when workers are hurt or killed, the cost of providing protective equipment free to workers, and new OSHA compliance obligations for state and local governments that currently operate their own programs or none at all.

drawbacks.text: Higher civil and criminal penalties raise the cost of doing business, a burden that falls hardest on small employers with thin margins, and the jump from a maximum six-month sentence to ten or twenty years for a willful violation causing death is a major expansion of criminal law [S3].

Extending OSHA to state and local government employees shifts compliance costs onto public budgets and could conflict with existing state safety programs, which the bill addresses by letting the Labor Secretary cede jurisdiction to other federal agencies whose standards are equally protective [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The scales tip toward workers. Federal OSHA's civil penalties had not been raised since 1990, so a maximum $7,000 fine for a serious violation was often cheaper for an employer than fixing the hazard, and a six-month maximum sentence for a willful violation killing a worker was rarely enforced as a deterrent [S3]. The costs are real but conventional: compliance spending on equipment and safety management is the normal cost of operating a workplace safely. The main honest criticism is design, not direction — the criminal penalty expansion is broad, and extending OSHA over public employees raises federalism questions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went from the House to the Education and Labor Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee in 2007, and stayed there; it never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey introduced the bill on April 26, 2007, with 72 House members — all Democrats — signing on as cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].

The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced, and in July 2007 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; the record shows no further action through the end of the 110th Congress [S5].
Democrats held the House majority and the committee chairmanship during this period, so the bill stalled despite its sponsors' party controlling the committee it was assigned to [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced civil fines up to $250,000 per violation, criminal exposure measured in years, and the cost of providing free protective equipment were better off because the bill never came to a vote. Government workers left outside OSHA's coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided higher safety penalties

for.name: Rep. Lynn Woolsey
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Labor Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor [S1][S5].

for.name: 72 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. George Miller of California, who was listed among the original sponsors [S3][S4].

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and never scheduled a markup or a vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress [S5].

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to raise OSHA penalties and expand coverage, arguing higher fines and criminal exposure burden employers.

sides.party_line_note: All 72 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill never reached a floor vote, so there was no roll call to measure the final split [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers subject to OSHA (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, and other hazardous industries)
industries.note: The bill multiplies the financial consequences of safety violations — fines up to $250,000 when a worker dies and prison sentences up to 20 years for repeat willful offenders — and adds the cost of free protective equipment [S3]. Its interest in lower penalties and lighter enforcement runs against workers' interest in safe workplaces.

industries.industry: State and local governments as employers
industries.note: Public agencies would become subject to federal OSHA enforcement, fines, and equipment requirements for the first time, a new cost for taxpayer-funded budgets [S3]. The bill lets the Labor Secretary cede jurisdiction where another agency's protections are equivalent, softening the impact [S3].
